# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles 44.223 settlements (353.744 settlement-year observations, mean 8 per centre) spanning urban centres, prefectural capitals, county seats, Special Administrative Region cores, Taiwanese townships, historical market towns and traditional villages active across the People's Republic of China, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao between 1949AD and 2026AD (9.389.222 km²). Drawing systematically upon seven national population censuses conducted in 1953AD, 1964AD, 1982AD, 1990AD, 2000AD, 2010AD and 2020AD, supplemented by National Bureau of Statistics yearbooks, province-disambiguated city and county census alignments anchored to CHGIS/MCGD [@Henriot2026MCGD], MOHURD Traditional Ancient Villages [@MOHURD2023TraditionalVillages], Taiwan Ministry of the Interior household registries, Hong Kong Census and Statistics Department digests and Macao Statistics and Census Service returns [@nbs1954census; @nbs1964census; @nbs1982census; @nbs1990census; @nbs2000census; @nbs2010census; @nbs2020census; @taiwan_moi2025; @hk_censtatd2025; @macao_dsec2025], the gazetteer covers all 34 provincial-level territories with province-verified geocoding and unbroken continuity across 1953AD to 2025AD. Coverage ranges from dense regional networks in Sichuan (2.702 sites), Hebei (2.609), Hunan (2.446) and Shanxi (2.422) to compact provincial-level municipalities and island territories. At the 2020AD to 2025AD benchmarks, the urban hierarchy is led by Chongqing (23,6M in 2025AD), Shanghai (22,83M), Beijing (20,08M), Shenzhen (18,61M), Chengdu (17,48M), Guangzhou (17,06M), Tianjin (12,33M), Suzhou (11,04M), Wuhan (11,02M), Xi'an (10,87M), Hangzhou (10,54M), Zhengzhou (10,47M) and Dongguan (10,22M) [@nbs2020census; @Peng2024More]. Alongside the 44.223 included centres, the regional source ledger archives 2.500 excluded candidates across 46.723 ledger-evaluated entries (following 12.252 raw co-located merges and exclusions, with 0 unaccounted records), consolidating close-proximity satellite nodes into canonical entries.

# Background

Urbanisation across China over the post-1949 period represents one of the largest demographic transformations in global history [@hou2001zhongguo; @Meng2019Rural]. In 1949AD, the vast majority of the Chinese population resided in agricultural villages, with modern manufacturing concentrated in treaty ports such as Shanghai, Tianjin, Qingdao and Guangzhou, alongside Japanese-developed industrial hubs in Liaoning (Shenyang, Dalian, Anshan) [@hou2001zhongguo; @nbs1954census]. Under early socialist central planning during the First Five-Year Plan (1953AD to 1957AD), state investment expanded heavy industrial bases across the Northeast Rustbelt and Central China, drawing millions of rural labourers into municipal state-owned enterprises [@nbs1954census; @Cheng2021Great].

To control rural-urban migration and manage food rationing following the disruptions of the Great Leap Forward famine (1959AD to 1961AD), the PRC government instituted strict enforcement of the dual household registration (*hukou*) system in 1958AD, dividing citizens into agricultural and non-agricultural statuses [@Song2009Does; @Meng2010Institutional; @Zhou2025Rural]. Urban expansion was further redirected by the Third Front construction campaign during the 1960s and 1970s, which relocated industrial plants and skilled personnel inland into mountainous recesses of Sichuan, Guizhou, Yunnan and Shaanxi [@Cheng2021Great].

The advent of economic reforms after 1978AD fundamentally reshaped this geography [@Meng2019Rural]. The creation of Special Economic Zones in Guangdong (Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Shantou) and Fujian (Xiamen), followed by the opening of coastal cities in 1984AD and the development of the Shanghai Pudong New Area in 1990AD, generated unprecedented rural-to-urban labour mobility [@Chen2019Polycentricity; @Zhang2017Multiplex]. Tens of millions of rural migrant workers (*nongmingong*) moved from inland agrarian provinces (Henan, Sichuan, Anhui, Jiangxi, Hunan) into coastal industrial corridors [@Meng2019Rural; @Chen2011Rural]. Shenzhen grew from a small border market town in Bao'an County into a global manufacturing and technology metropolis of 18,61M inhabitants [@Chen2019Polycentricity; @Li2017Urban]. Concurrently, Taiwan underwent rapid industrialisation and urban concentration along its western coastal plain from Taipei and New Taipei down to Taichung and Kaohsiung [@taiwan_moi2025], while Hong Kong absorbed waves of mainland migrants to form a high-density international financial centre of 7,54M [@hk_censtatd2025; @Almond2007Long], and Macao expanded through maritime land reclamation into a global hospitality hub of 690k [@macao_dsec2025].

# Methodology

Urban population figures were assembled from official decennial tabulations of the State Statistical Bureau and National Bureau of Statistics of China for the 1953AD, 1964AD, 1982AD, 1990AD, 2000AD, 2010AD and 2020AD censuses [@nbs1954census; @nbs1964census; @nbs1982census; @nbs1990census; @nbs2000census; @nbs2010census; @nbs2020census], complemented by municipal statistical yearbooks, published 2025AD administrative counts, and province-disambiguated city and county census alignments anchored to CHGIS/MCGD [@Henriot2026MCGD] and the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development National Directory of Chinese Traditional Villages [@MOHURD2023TraditionalVillages]. Historical CHGIS market towns and Traditional Ancient Villages are carried forward continuously across 1953AD to 2025AD, yielding 353.744 settlement-year observations across 44.223 centres (mean 8 per centre). Taiwanese settlements draw upon Ministry of the Interior household registration statistics [@taiwan_moi2025], Hong Kong figures draw upon Census and Statistics Department reports [@hk_censtatd2025], and Macao records draw upon Direcção dos Serviços de Estatística e Censos tabulations [@macao_dsec2025].

Geographic coordinates reflect canonical WGS84 locations for prefectural administrative centres, county seats, municipal districts, market towns and traditional villages. Province-verified geocoding and spatial snapping reconcile settlement coordinates against the 34 provincial boundary masks. In the regional source ledger, 2.500 excluded duplicate or co-located candidates out of 46.723 ledger-evaluated entries (following 12.252 raw co-located merges and exclusions, with 0 unaccounted records) were consolidated into higher-ranking municipal centres (for example, satellite urban county designations consolidated into Dongguan, Xiantao, Tianmen, Qianjiang, Jiyuan, Wenchang and Basuo) to maintain strict demographic consistency.

# Testing and Validation

Cross-ledger auditing verifies exact reconciliation across all 46.723 ledger-evaluated entries: 44.223 active included settlements (353.744 settlement-year observations, mean 8 per centre), 2.500 excluded duplicate entries archived in the ledger (alongside 12.252 raw co-located merges and exclusions) and 0 unaccounted records. Every catalogued settlement possesses non-zero population observations spanning the 1949AD to 2026AD temporal domain and valid province-verified WGS84 coordinates. Figure \ref{fig:sett-prc} presents the rank-size distribution and the leading fifteen settlement peaks.

# Limitations

Three administrative and methodological factors condition settlement population series in contemporary China. First, the boundary definition of Chinese cities has evolved substantially over the reform era [@Petushkova2025Urbanization; @Zhong2022Urban]. Administrative municipalities (*shi*) encompass both densely built-up urban districts (*shi-xia-qu*) and extensive surrounding rural counties and county-level cities. For megacities such as Chongqing, the total municipal population exceeds 32M across 82.400 km², whereas the built-up urban core accommodates 23,6M [@Peng2024More]. Second, official statistics distinguish between registered *hukou* inhabitants and permanent resident populations (*changzhurenkou*) living in an urban centre for six months or longer [@Meng2019Rural; @Zhou2025Rural]. Post-2000 national censuses capture permanent residents regardless of registration status, reflecting true de facto urban concentrations [@nbs2000census; @nbs2020census]. Third, integrating province-disambiguated PRC city and county census alignments anchored to CHGIS/MCGD [@Henriot2026MCGD] with MOHURD Traditional Ancient Villages [@MOHURD2023TraditionalVillages] carries forward all historical market towns and traditional villages continuously across 1953AD to 2025AD with province-verified geocoding (44.223 included sites and 353.744 settlement-year observations, mean 8 per centre), while archiving 2.500 excluded candidates in the ledger (following 12.252 raw co-located merges and exclusions across 46.723 evaluated entries) to prevent spatial double-counting.
